held_case_resolutions.rationale: MA statutory §20(c) gives 2 days for ordinary oral electronic follow-up, and 7 calendar days for written follow-up under a commissioner eRx exception, while DPH 105 CMR 721.070(B) provides seven business days for oral II–V under 721.070(A). The exact deadline hierarchy remains not harmonized. Original item was rewritten so no choice asks one deadline; it instead tests oral legitimacy, required subsequent documentation/record linkage, and pharmacist exception-checking duty.

option_verdicts.explanation: Correct. 105 CMR 721.070(A)(2) expressly permits an oral or written prescription during temporary technological or electrical failure. Federal 21 CFR 1306.21 generally allows lawful Schedule IV oral orders when ordinary authenticity and prescription requirements are satisfied.

Incorrect. M.G.L. c.94C §20(c) imposes a subsequent prescription duty for oral Schedule II–V prescriptions, and 105 CMR 721.070(B) implements follow-up for oral prescriptions issued under ePrescribing exceptions. No universal absence of follow-up can be inferred from federal Schedule IV rules.

Correct. The follow-up and pharmacy record-attachment duties are supported by M.G.L. c.94C §20(c) and 105 CMR 721.070(B). The statute describes a two-day electronic default or seven-calendar-day written exception, whereas the DPH implementing rule uses seven BUSINESS days for an ePrescribing exception. Because these differ, this question deliberately does not assert one universal deadline; practitioners should comply with applicable requirements and obtain agency clarification when necessary.

Correct. 105 CMR 721.070(C) specifically relieves the pharmacist from verifying the qualifying ePrescribing exception. That narrow exception does not excuse pharmacist verification of an oral prescription's lawful source or medical legitimacy.

held_case_resolutions.rationale: Original 17-year-old/50kg/no-refill scenario depended on inaccessible September 2026 state pharmacist PEP DOCX; the original patient-specific claims were not certified. Revised to an adult with explicitly assumed statewide-protocol eligibility, testing urgency and a 28-day course supported by CDC 2025 and MA DPH's Aug2026 pharmacist-prescribing circular. Does not verify pediatric or precise state supply limit.

option_verdicts.explanation: Incorrect. CDC 2025 nPEP recommendations emphasize starting indicated PEP as soon as possible, no later than 72 hours, without delaying the first dose for pending laboratory results. Baseline HIV testing should still be obtained promptly and interpreted.

Incorrect. M.G.L. c.94C §19F and Massachusetts DPH Circular DCP 26-08-125 independently authorize appropriately qualified pharmacists to prescribe specified HIV prevention medications under statewide guidance. A separate patient-specific CDTM agreement is not inherently required for that distinct authority.

Incorrect. An exposure that occurred 36 hours ago calls for the PEP pathway when clinically indicated. PEP is a 28-day course with baseline and follow-up testing; it is not interchangeable with routine PrEP, which is intended for prospective prevention.

Correct. CDC 2025 nPEP recommendations support starting eligible patients' 28-day PEP as soon as possible within 72 hours without waiting for pending laboratory test results, while still performing baseline and follow-up HIV evaluation. M.G.L. c.94C §19F and DPH Circular DCP 26-08-125 authorize appropriately qualified Massachusetts pharmacists to prescribe covered HIV-prevention medications under statewide guidance. The stem explicitly assumes other state-protocol eligibility requirements are met.

held_case_resolutions.rationale: Board mandatory disclosure form and 247 CMR 20.03 require reporting arrests and out-of-state discipline within 14 calendar days, but §10.03(1)(y)-(z) independently makes failure to report qualifying discipline and final license actions within seven business days a disciplinary ground. Rewrite best answer B to satisfy 14-calendar and any applicable shorter seven-business period. Do not claim 14 days supersedes §10.03.

option_verdicts.explanation: Incorrect. 247 CMR 20.03(3) separately requires reporting any arrest, pending charge, or conviction. Out-of-state professional discipline is also reportable under §20.03(4) and can trigger the additional reporting provisions in §10.03.

Correct. 247 CMR 20.03(3)-(4) expressly provides 14 calendar days for arrests and reportable discipline. Separately, §10.03(1)(y)-(z) lists failure to report qualifying discipline or governmental final actions within seven business days as a possible disciplinary ground. A pharmacist must not assume that the 14-day provision universally overrides this potentially earlier duty; the exact action and deadlines should be assessed together.
Incorrect. Neither §20.03 nor §10.03 authorizes waiting for renewal, and the §10.03 reporting duties may extend to acts of other licensing authorities.

Incorrect. §§20.03(3)-(4) address individual licensee duties directly. The separate §10.03 seven-business-day requirement concerns qualifying disciplinary and governmental actions, not a generic seven-day arrest rule. §10.03(1)(aa) also addresses pending charges or convictions on a different clock.
